Mark each page with the most specific entity in each lineage

Each page should list only its most specific entities. A musician who is also a knowledge gardener lists Logseq/Entity/Person/Musician and Logseq/Entity/Person/Knowledge Gardener and leaves out Logseq/Entity/Person, because each of those is already a kind of person. Musician, then Person, is one lineage: an entity followed by each entity it is a kind of. This narrows the hypothesis codekiln wrote in the 2026-10-01 Thu journal: the rule covers only a child entity that is a kind of its parent, and it lets one page carry two sibling entities. The Musician, Knowledge Gardener and User Guide definition pages currently say to mark each instance with the parent entity as well.

Mark each page with the most specific entity in each lineage

I recommend lineage: an entity and its chain of is-a parents up to the topmost defined entity, so a musician's lineage is Musician, then Person. It is an ordinary word, it reads well in a rule ("two entities in one lineage"), and it leaves out part-of children, since an episode does not descend from a show. Clade names the group in the other direction: Person together with every entity that descends from it, Musician and Knowledge Gardener included.

Class inheritance is a model for how a child entity takes rules from its parents in one lineage. A child definition page works like a subclass: it inherits the parent's page shape and states only its deviations, which is My/Principle/Simplify/Don't Repeat Yourself DRY applied to definitions. Several unrelated markers on one page are like Software/Inheritance/Multiple. When two of a page's entities give conflicting rules, whoever edits the page follows the entity listed first, the way Python looks up a method in a class's parents in the order they are listed.
Mark each page with the most specific entity in each lineage

CSS class selectors are a model for how the rules of two entities on one page combine. A page's markers act like an element's classes, class="episode youtube". Rules written for .episode and for .youtube both apply. A rule written for .episode.youtube applies only when both classes are present, and it wins over either alone because it is more specific (MDN on specificity). The combination needs no hierarchy.
Mark each page with the most specific entity in each lineage

CSS also has a separate inheritance along the document tree, where a child element takes some property values from its parent element (MDN on inheritance). That matches part-of. An episode can take its created-by:: and its subject from the show it files under without being a kind of show.
Mark each page with the most specific entity in each lineage

Taken together: a child entity inherits from its ancestors the way a subclass does, a rule written for a combination applies the way a CSS rule for .episode.youtube does, and an episode takes defaults from its show the way an HTML element inherits CSS properties from its parent. Pages in the garden already follow each of these: the Logseq/Entity/Book/Section levels, the Logseq/Entity/Trade-Off page shape, and episodes filed under their show. An entity system built on subclassing, CSS selectors and CSS inheritance would describe how the garden already works.

This property says whether a child entity is a kind of its parent or a part of it, and it goes on the child's definition page, the one whose name nests under the parent's. Every blog post is an article, so the Logseq/Entity/Article/Blog definition page, which nests under Logseq/Entity/Article, would carry logseq-entity-hierarchy-type:: [[Logseq/Entity/Hierarchy/Frontmatter/Type/extends]].

The child entity is a kind of its parent: every instance of the child is also an instance of the parent, and the child definition page states only how its instances differ from the parent's. Logseq/Entity/Person/Maker extends Logseq/Entity/Person, and Logseq/Entity/Article/Blog extends Logseq/Entity/Article.

The child entity is a different thing that belongs to an instance of its parent. An episode belongs to a show, so Logseq/Entity/Podcast/Episode is part of Logseq/Entity/Podcast, and one page is never both a show and one of its episodes. Whoever files a part-of instance usually puts its page under the page of the thing it belongs to, so an episode's page goes in its show's Pod namespace, as Hard Fork/Pod/26/09/A.I. Safety Goes Mainstream + a ‘Hard Fork’ Exit AMA sits under Hard Fork/Pod.
In this garden, Identity pages model a public name under which a person or collective publishes, performs or makes work.
A stage name, pen name, named artistic project or collective with a recognizable body of work. The identity has a page separate from the biographical people behind it.
A person's ordinary biographical name alone does not require a second page. A spelling variant or abbreviation that names the same identity can remain an alias.
A shared credit does not by itself establish a new collective identity. A collaboration can credit several existing identities.
Use the published name as a short page title, such as Bibio. Entity classification belongs in frontmatter, rather than in an Identity/ prefix on every instance.
Add a disambiguating namespace only when the published name collides with another page.
Mark an instance with its most specific identity entity; a Band instance leaves Identity and Music Identity out of logseq-entity::.
A person can have several identities, and a collective identity can have several people behind it. Identity pages carry identity entities; biographical pages carry person or maker entities.
Logseq/Entity/Identity/Frontmatter/identity-of links an identity to known people behind it. Unknown people are left unstated.
Logseq/Frontmatter/created-by-identities links a work or release to its credited identities. A link to an identity does not imply that every associated person contributed to every work.
A work's created-by:: links the known people who made that particular work. Identity membership alone is insufficient evidence for a personal credit.
Search published names, existing titles, aliases, official URLs and person-page mentions before creating an identity.

When the identity exists only as an alias on a person page, retain the biographical page and separate the identity from that alias before creating its page. Other aliases and the person's biographical information remain with the person.
Older pages under Group/ can already represent collective identities. Their existing titles remain valid until deliberately renamed.
One linked H1 with the published name and official URL when known, a short description, and verified links to the people behind the identity.
The shared attribution property is linked above; domain-specific placement of works and recordings is defined by the corresponding identity child and work entity.

In this garden, Music Identity pages model the public artist or project names under which music is released or performed.
Naming, person relationships, deduplication and marking follow Logseq/Entity/Identity. A Music Identity is an identity, not a biographical musician.
A recording's Logseq/Frontmatter/created-by-identities lists the identities credited on the release, in published order.
Place releases under the first credited identity as <Identity>/Music/Recording/<Title>, following Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording. A joint release has one page and lists every credited identity.

Place a separately represented composition under its primary credited identity as <Identity>/Music/Work/<Title>, following Logseq/Entity/Music/Work. A recording's artist credit does not establish the composition's authorship.
Personal credits still link the people who actually wrote, produced or performed the music, following Logseq/Entity/Person/Maker.
Bibio and Dorian Concept are solo music identities, each linked to a separate person hub.
Bibio/Music/Recording/Answers credits both identities without creating a separate identity for their collaboration.
In this garden, Band pages model music identities shared by musicians working as a named band.
Attribution and release placement follow Logseq/Entity/Identity/Music, which inherits Logseq/Entity/Identity. A Band instance carries only the Band entity from this lineage.
A band's identity and release namespace persist through changes of membership. Albums belong under the band, rather than under an individual member.

Known people can be linked through Logseq/Entity/Identity/Frontmatter/identity-of. Membership periods, instruments and roles belong in dated body blocks when known; an undated person link makes no claim about current membership.
A recording lists individual participants only when their participation on that recording is known. Neither a current nor a historical membership list establishes a recording credit.
A one-off joint credit is not automatically a band. A named project receives a Band page when it has a band identity of its own.

In this garden, Keyshort pages model a keyboard shortcut: a key, key combination, or key sequence that invokes an action in a particular tool or environment.
An action-specific page under a tool or environment namespace, usually shaped as Scope/Keyshort/Action or Scope/Keyshort/Subscope/Action.
Alternative bindings for the same action may share one page. Closely related actions may share a page when they are reviewed together as a group.
Individual physical or logical keys are Logseq/Entity/Key instances.
A command entered as text is a Logseq/Entity/CLI/Command instance; a Keyshort may invoke that command.
Scope/Keyshort and subscope pages organize shortcuts. Action leaves are the Keyshort instances.
The page name starts with the tool or environment scope, followed by Keyshort and a concise action phrase: Scope/Keyshort/Action.
An optional subscope sits between Keyshort and the action: Scope/Keyshort/Subscope/Action.
The same chord in different scopes represents different Keyshorts because its action and context may differ.
Match the scope and action first, then compare the bindings and descriptions.
Multiple bindings for one action belong on the same page. The same binding for different actions remains separate.
Keyshort pages use the logseq-entity:: property with Logseq/Entity/Keyshort.

The page carries Keyshort and enough scope links for the relevant {{cards}} queries to find it, either on the review prompt or on a parent block.

Alternative bindings for one action appear as sibling answer blocks beneath the same prompt.

Proxying an entity instance brings along the entity definitions and executable tasks needed to use it in the destination garden. Running sync again updates those pages and task files from the same source.

A copy of Logseq/Entity/Proxy/Page brings its entity definitions, sync executable, and runtime helpers into another garden. The copied task runs through mise and re-syncs the destination.
In this garden, Mise Task pages model named jobs supplied by a repository or configuration scope and invoked through mise.
A task is identified by its owning repository or configuration collection, config root, and exact task name. Identical names in separate repositories or config roots identify separate tasks.
The task definition can be an executable file or a TOML task. A helper module, package, fixture, or test file becomes part of a task's implementation rather than a separate task entity.
Built-in mise subcommands such as mise run are Logseq/Entity/CLI/Command instances. Jobs invoked through them are Mise Task instances.

Task reference pages belong to the topic served by the job: Topic/mise/Task/<task-name-with-colons-as-slashes>. A namespace prefix already expressed by the topic can be omitted from the page name while remaining in task-name::.

For example, logseq:entity:proxy:page:sync lives at Logseq/Entity/Proxy/Page/mise/Task/sync: the topic already expresses logseq:entity:proxy:page. Repository ownership remains explicit in frontmatter.
If the topic contains distinct implementations of the same task name, add a repository or config-scope segment before the task path. Displayed invocation text retains the exact runnable name.
logseq-entity:: marks the page as a Mise Task instance.
task-owner:: links the owning repository or configuration collection.
